title: Equity in the Use of ChatGPT for the Classroom: A Comparison of the Accuracy and Precision of ChatGPT 3.5 vs. ChatGPT4 with Respect to Statistics and Data Science Exams
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether students who rely on the free version of ChatGPT (ChatGPT 3.5) are disadvantaged relative to students who can pay for ChatGPT4 when using generative AI for statistics and data science learning. The central question is an equity one: if paid and free versions differ substantially in accuracy and response quality, then generative AI could widen rather than reduce educational inequality. The authors frame this in relation to social mobility, the digital divide, and the growing use of AI tools by students even when classroom policies restrict them.

The study compares ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT4 by entering the same statistics questions, one at a time, into each platform and grading the outputs. The question set consisted of 93 items drawn from four exams at different levels: the Arkansas Council of Teachers of Mathematics exam, the CAOS exam, the 2011 AP Statistics exam, and a first-year graduate statistical methods exam for PhD students in statistics, biostatistics, and data science. Questions included multiple-choice and free-response formats, with and without images. Responses were scored using a rubric, then compared using McNemar's test for dichotomized correctness and ordinal logistic regression for quality differences.

The educational context spans high school statistics, introductory college statistics, AP-level statistics, and graduate-level statistical methods, but the paper does not study students interacting with the tool directly in an instructional intervention. Instead, it treats exam performance as a proxy for the quality of tutoring or study assistance a student might receive. The study was conducted by researchers in the Department of Statistics and Data Science at Southern Methodist University in the United States.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT4 consistently outperformed ChatGPT 3.5 across all exams and question types. ChatGPT4 answered 80% of all questions correctly versus 50% for ChatGPT 3.5, and the gap was especially large for image-based questions because ChatGPT 3.5 could not interpret images. The authors argue that this performance gap creates an equity concern: students who cannot afford paid AI access may receive poorer instructional support. They also note that the study is limited by sample size, single-institution authorship/context, lack of direct student-use data, and the fact that the analyzed version landscape became outdated as newer models were released.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot family used for question answering and assistance across text and image-enabled tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper compared ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4 on 93 statistics and data science exam questions from ACTM, CAOS, AP Statistics, and a first-year graduate methods exam, grading accuracy and response quality on multiple-choice and free-response items with and without images.

findings.finding_summary: Across all 93 statistics/data science exam questions, ChatGPT4 outperformed ChatGPT3.5 on paired accuracy. ChatGPT4 answered 80% (76/93) correctly versus 50% (47/93) for ChatGPT3.5; McNemar's test on discordant pairs gave χ2_1 = 19.9, p = .000012, with 35 questions correct for ChatGPT4 and incorrect for ChatGPT3.5 versus 6 in the opposite direction.
findings.measure: Correct vs incorrect answers on 93 paired exam questions across four statistics/data science exams

findings.finding_summary: On questions without images, ChatGPT4 showed higher paired accuracy than ChatGPT3.5. ChatGPT4 answered 88% of non-image questions correctly versus 71% for ChatGPT3.5; among discordant pairs, 17 favored ChatGPT4 and 6 favored ChatGPT3.5, with McNemar p = .03.
findings.measure: Correct vs incorrect answers on questions without images

findings.finding_summary: On questions with images, ChatGPT4 substantially outperformed ChatGPT3.5. ChatGPT4 answered 66% (20/30) of image-based questions correctly versus 6% (2/30) for ChatGPT3.5; discordant pairs were 18 favoring ChatGPT4 and 0 favoring ChatGPT3.5, with McNemar p = .00006.
findings.measure: Correct vs incorrect answers on image-based questions

findings.finding_summary: For free-response questions, ChatGPT4 had higher accuracy than ChatGPT3.5 after dichotomizing scores as correct if >=3 on the rubric. ChatGPT4 answered 82% (23/28) correctly versus 43% (12/28) for ChatGPT3.5; McNemar's test gave p = .010, with 18 discordant questions favoring ChatGPT4 and 2 favoring ChatGPT3.5.
findings.measure: Correct vs incorrect on free-response questions scored with a 0-4 rubric and dichotomized at >=3

findings.finding_summary: For multiple-choice questions, ChatGPT4 outperformed ChatGPT3.5 on paired accuracy. The paper reports McNemar p = .0009, with 22 discordant questions favoring ChatGPT4 and 4 favoring ChatGPT3.5.
findings.measure: Correct vs incorrect answers on multiple-choice questions

findings.finding_summary: Ordinal logistic regression on response quality differences found that image presence strongly increased ChatGPT4's advantage over ChatGPT3.5. The Image Present coefficient was 1.9172 (SE = 0.4599, z = 4.169, p = 3.06 x 10^-5), corresponding to an estimated 580% increase in the odds that ChatGPT4 would provide a higher-quality response; the paper states a 95% confidence interval for the increase in odds between 276% and 1575%.
findings.measure: Quality difference in responses on a 0-4 ordinal scoring rubric modeled by ordinal logistic regression
findings.confidence_interval: 95% CI for increase in odds: 276% to 1575%

findings.finding_summary: Ordinal logistic regression did not find sufficient evidence that free-response versus multiple-choice format changed ChatGPT4's advantage over ChatGPT3.5 after controlling for image presence. The TypeFR coefficient was 0.4565 (SE = 0.4538, z = 1.006, p = 0.314439), which the authors interpret as an estimated 57% increase in odds with a 95% confidence interval ranging from a 35.2% decrease to a 284% increase.
findings.measure: Effect of question type on quality difference between ChatGPT4 and ChatGPT3.5 in ordinal logistic regression
findings.confidence_interval: 95% CI for percent change in odds: -35.2% to 284%

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical comparative study of a named AI tool using paired exam-item analyses, but it is not a student learning intervention, RCT, or QED with learners assigned to tool conditions. Outcomes are tool performance on exam questions rather than direct student outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear performance differences favoring ChatGPT4 over ChatGPT3.5, especially for image-based statistics questions, but it does not report standardized educational effect sizes or direct impacts on students' learning. Impact on education is therefore suggestive but indirect and unclear.
